## What you'll learn

- How to predict genes in metagenomic assemblies, and why metagenomes need a special mode.
- What Prodigal's output files contain.
- Why genes at the edges of contigs are a problem, and how we handle them.

## The data

The workshop has three small metagenomes (`metag1`–`metag3`). Their reads have already been quality-controlled and assembled with metaSPAdes, and scaffolds shorter than 500 bp were removed. You'll find:

```text
data/scaffolds/metag1.scaffolds.min500.fasta   assembled scaffolds, one file per sample
data/reads/metag1.1.fq.gz, metag1.2.fq.gz       forward and reverse reads (used in Part C)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## How were the assemblies made?
With the commands from the [metagenomic assembly protocol](https://methods-in-microbiomics.readthedocs.io/en/latest/assembly/metagenomic_workflows.html):

```{.bash .notest}
metaspades.py -t 4 -m 12 --only-assembler \
  --pe1-1 reads/metag1.1.fq.gz --pe1-2 reads/metag1.2.fq.gz -o asm/metag1
python scaffold_filter.py metag1 scaffolds asm/metag1/scaffolds.fasta asm/metag1 META
```

The full recipe is in `data-prep/gene-catalogs/prepare.sh` in the repository.
:::

Take a look at the first scaffold names in the terminal:

```bash
grep ">" data/scaffolds/metag1.scaffolds.min500.fasta | head -3
grep -c ">" data/scaffolds/*.fasta
```

The scaffold filter has renamed the scaffolds to `<sample>-scaffold_<n>`. Because the sample name is part of every scaffold name, gene names will stay unique when we pool all samples in Part B.

## Predict genes with Prodigal

[Prodigal](https://github.com/hyattpd/Prodigal) finds protein-coding genes by learning what genes look like in the input (codon usage, start codons, ribosome binding sites). Its default mode trains on a single genome. A metagenomic assembly contains many genomes, and most scaffolds are too short to train on, so we use the **metagenomic mode** (`-p meta`): pre-trained models from many reference genomes.

```bash
mkdir -p genes
for s in metag1 metag2 metag3; do
  prodigal -p meta -c -q \
    -i data/scaffolds/$s.scaffolds.min500.fasta \
    -a genes/$s.faa -d genes/$s.fna -f gff -o genes/$s.gff
done
ls genes
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-p meta` | Metagenomic mode: use pre-trained gene models instead of training on the input |
| `-c` | Closed ends: don't allow genes to run off the edges of a scaffold |
| `-q` | Quiet: don't print progress |
| `-i` | Input FASTA file |
| `-a` | Write protein translations (amino acids) to this file |
| `-d` | Write gene nucleotide sequences to this file |
| `-f gff` / `-o` | Write gene coordinates in GFF format to this file |

## Look at the output

Prodigal writes three files per sample. The **GFF** file lists where each gene is:

{{< include data/_excerpts/gff.md >}}

The **protein** file (`.faa`) has one sequence per gene. The header holds the coordinates, the strand, and extra information:

{{< include data/_excerpts/faa.md >}}

The header fields are separated by `#`: gene name, start, end, strand (`1` forward, `-1` reverse), then attributes. Gene names are `<scaffold>_<n>`, so `metag1-scaffold_1_1` is the first gene on scaffold 1 of metag1. The `.fna` file has the same genes as nucleotide sequences.

Count the genes per sample:

```bash
grep -c ">" genes/*.faa
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected output
```text
genes/metag1.faa:798
genes/metag2.faa:899
genes/metag3.faa:807
```
:::

## Explore the genes

The table `genes.csv` contains the information from all `.faa` headers of the reference run. Explore it here in the browser:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#| edit: false
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
theme_set(theme_bw())
genes <- read_csv("data/genes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{webr}
genes

ggplot(genes, aes(length_nt)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50) +
  labs(x = "Gene length (nt)", y = "Number of genes")
```

### Exercise: start codons

Most bacterial genes start with ATG, but not all. Count how many genes use each start codon (`start_type`). What fraction start with ATG?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_start
genes %>%
  count(______) %>%
  mutate(fraction = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_start"}
`count()` takes the name of the column to count.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_start"}
```r
genes %>%
  count(start_type) %>%
  mutate(fraction = n / sum(n))
```
About 85% start with ATG, about 11% with GTG and 5% with TTG, typical for bacteria.
:::

## Genes at the edges: the `partial` field

Metagenomic assemblies are fragmented, so many genes are cut off by the end of a scaffold. Prodigal reports this in the `partial` attribute: `00` means complete, `10` means the gene runs off the left edge, `01` the right edge.

```{webr}
genes %>% count(partial)
```

All genes are complete because we used `-c`, which makes Prodigal drop genes that would run off an edge.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
import {quiz} from "../../assets/quiz.ojs"

quiz("Using -c removes genes cut off at scaffold edges. What's the trade-off?", [
  {text: "There's no trade-off: partial genes are always wrong", correct: false, why: "Partial genes are usually real genes; we just don't have all of them."},
  {text: "We lose some real genes, especially on short scaffolds, but every gene in the catalog is complete", correct: true, why: "Complete genes cluster more reliably in Part B, and gene length normalisation in Part D assumes full-length genes. The price is missing genes in highly fragmented assemblies."},
  {text: "Prodigal runs faster", correct: false, why: "Speed is not the reason; it's about the quality of the catalog."}
])
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
quiz("Why do we run Prodigal with -p meta on metagenomic assemblies?", [
  {text: "It's faster", correct: false, why: "Speed isn't the point."},
  {text: "A metagenome contains many genomes, and its scaffolds are too short to train a single-genome model on", correct: true, why: "In meta mode, Prodigal uses pre-trained models from many reference genomes and picks the best one for each scaffold."},
  {text: "It finds RNA genes too", correct: false, why: "Prodigal only predicts protein-coding genes in both modes."}
])
```

## Check your work

In the terminal:

```bash
./check a
```

## Key points

- Use Prodigal's **metagenomic mode** (`-p meta`) for assemblies with many genomes.
- Sample-prefixed scaffold names keep gene names unique when samples are pooled.
- `-c` keeps only complete genes, so the catalog contains no partial genes.
